## Part 3


Q1: the given operators are somewhat related to eachother, the first operator prints the qoutient with a decimal, the second operator prints only the remainder and the third operator prints the integer
```{r}
10 %% 3
10 %/% 3
```
Q2: I predicted the result would be 1 because  %%  is the modulo operator in R, which calculates the remainder when the first number is divided by the second. It works by finding how many times 3 fits evenly into 10-exactly 3 times, which totals 9. Subtracting 9 from 10 leaves 1, so that is the remainder. The spaces around the operator do not affect its function, so both expressions give the same answer.

```{r}
x <- 42
class(x)
y <- 42L
class(y)
z <- "42"
class(z)
w <- TRUE
class(w)
v <- 3 + 2i 
class(v) 
```

```{r}
x <- 42
mode(x)
y <- 42L
mode(y)
z <- "42"
mode(z)
w <- TRUE
mode(w)
v <- 3 + 2i 
mode(v) 
```

Q#3: So, while 42 and 42L look the same when printed, under the hood one is a floating-point number and the other is a true integer.
